q-15638.name: Question 1
q-15638.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\frac{x+1}{x}$ about $x=5$ is
q-15638.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=5,$ we plug $a=5$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(5)+{f}^{′}(5)(x-5)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(5)(x-5)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(5),$ ${f}^{′}(5),$ and ${f}^{″}(5):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+1}{x} & ⟹ &  & f(5) & =\frac{6}{5} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(5) & =-\frac{1}{25} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =2{x}^{-3} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(5) & =\frac{2}{125}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(5),$ ${f}^{′}(5),$ and ${f}^{″}(5)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =(\frac{6}{5})+(-\frac{1}{25})\cdot (x-5)+(\frac{2}{125})\cdot \frac{1}{2}(x-5)^{2} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}-\frac{1}{25}(x-5)+\frac{1}{125}(x-5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

The second-degree Taylor polynomial of f(x)=e−2x about x=0 is

a
1−2x+8x2
b
1−2x+4x2
c
1−2x+x28
d
1−2x+2x2
e
1−2x+x22
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about x=0, we plug a=0 into the general formula to give

P2(x)=f(0)+f′(0)(x−0)+12f″(0)(x−0)2.

So, we need to work out f(0), f′(0), and f″(0):

f(x)=e−2x⟹f(0)=1f′(x)=−2e−2x⟹f′(0)=−2f″(x)=4e−2x⟹f″(0)=4

We now plug the results for f(0), f′(0), and f″(0) into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

P2(x)=1+(−2)x+42x2=1−2x+2x2.

q-50683.problem: The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ about $x=4$ is
q-50683.worked_solution:
To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=4,$ we plug $a=4$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(4)+{f}^{′}(4)(x-4)+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(4)(x-4)^{2}.
$$

So, we need to work out $f(4),$ ${f}^{′}(4),$ and ${f}^{″}(4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{x}={x}^{1/2} & ⟹ &  & f(4) & =2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2} & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(4) & =-\frac{1}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

We now plug the results for $f(4),$ ${f}^{′}(4),$ and ${f}^{″}(4)$ into our second-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =2+\frac{1}{4}(x-4)-(\frac{1}{32})\cdot \frac{1}{2}(x-4)^{2} \\  & =2+\frac{1}{4}(x-4)-\frac{1}{64}(x-4)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=-4$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(-4)+{f}^{′}(-4)(x+4)+\frac{{f}^{″}(-4)}{2}(x+4)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $(x+4)^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{{f}^{″}(-4)}{2}.
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\sqrt{5-x}=(5-x)^{1/2} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}(5-x)^{-1/2} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\frac{1}{4}(5-x)^{-3/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=-4.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(-4) & =-\frac{1}{4}(5-(-4))^{-3/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\cdot {9}^{-3/2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{108}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $(x+4)^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(-4)}{2} & =\frac{(-\frac{1}{108})}{2}=-\frac{1}{216}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(\pi )+{f}^{′}(\pi )(x-\pi )+\frac{{f}^{″}(\pi )}{2}(x-\pi )^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of $(x-\pi )^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\pi ).
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\pi .$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(\pi )=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-(-1)=1.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of $(x-\pi )^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(\pi )}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$
